definition: Magnify means to make something appear larger or more important than it is.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word magnify. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know magnify should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The playoff loss was one of dozens; a decade without a trophy magnified it into a curse.
To overplay a stumble is to give it a bit more weight than it earned; magnify goes further — the stumble fills the frame and looms far larger than life.
Mythologize passes magnify: the event isn't just enlarged now, it has been rebuilt into legend, more story than fact.

To exaggerate is to stretch the claim itself — faster, bigger, worse than the facts support — and it lives in the telling. Magnify can work without a single word spoken: the thing's seeming size and importance swell while the facts underneath stay exactly as they were. Exaggeration bends the account; magnify bloats the image.

Dramatize means to retell events so they play bigger than life — a teller staging the scene for an audience, complete with peril and rescue. Magnify needs no performance and no audience; a worry magnified in one silent mind still swells. Dramatize is about the show; magnify is about the seeming size.

In 1918, a sheet of one hundred airmail stamps left the printing office with its blue airplane accidentally printed upside down.
As an error, it was trivial -- a misaligned plate, caught within days -- and the postal service simply corrected the plates and moved on.
Collectors did not move on.
Every article about the hobby retold the mistake, every auction of a single copy set records, and each retelling seemed to magnify the sheet's importance a little more.
A century later, one small printing error looms over the whole field: casual collectors who cannot name another rare stamp can describe the upside-down plane.
What grew was the space they filled in the hobby's imagination.
